items.title: Domestic violence against women in south asia and south-east asia: a comparative scoping review of prevalence, forms, and mental health outcomes.
items.authors: Gore M, Morgan J, Padhye Y, Kaplay V.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Domestic violence and abuse (DVA), including intimate partner violence (IPV), is a major public health concern with profound consequences for women's mental health. Evidence from South Asia (SA) and Southeast Asia (SEA) remains fragmented. This scoping review aimed to map the prevalence and forms of DVA experienced by women in these regions and synthesize evidence on associated mental health outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This review followed Arksey and O'Malley's scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Six electronic databases (SCOPUS, Web of Science, PubMed/MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and Google Scholar) were systematically searched for English-language studies published from 2015 onward. Search terms included domestic violence, intimate partner violence, women, South Asia, Southeast Asia, and mental health outcomes. Of 545 records identified, 270 remained after duplicate removal. Following title, abstract, and full-text screening, 23 studies met the inclusion criteria. Eligible studies included women aged ≥ 18 years from SA or SEA who had experienced any form of DVA and reported mental health outcomes. Studies unrelated to women, DVA, mental health outcomes, or conducted during emergencies or pandemics were excluded.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Domestic violence was highly prevalent across both regions, with lifetime prevalence generally ranging from 33%-51% in SA and 16%-63% in SEA. Women experienced multiple forms of abuse, including physical, psychological, sexual, economic abuse, neglect, and controlling behaviours, with psychological and emotional violence being the most frequently reported. Patriarchal gender norms, economic dependence, and unequal power relations consistently increased women's vulnerability, particularly among pregnant women, migrants, ethnic minorities, and rural women. Depression was the most common mental health consequence, followed by anxiety, psychological distress, suicidal ideation, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Women also reported social isolation, guilt, emotional dysregulation, reduced quality of life, and increased risks of psychiatric disorders.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: DVA is strongly associated with adverse mental health outcomes among women in SA and SEA, highlighting the need for integrated, culturally sensitive interventions. Routine screening for violence and mental health problems, strengthened support services, trauma-informed care, and further research on effective prevention and intervention strategies in primary care and community settings are essential to improve women's health and well-being.

items.title: Early-life parental income mobility and risk of depression and anxiety in adolescence and young adulthood among non-immigrants and second-generation immigrants.
items.authors: Okuyama K, Lönn SL, Hamano T, Khoshnood AM, Sundquist J, Sundquist K.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Little is known about the association between early-life income mobility patterns and the subsequent risk of depression/anxiety among immigrant populations. Understanding these associations may help identify persistent low income and declining income as potential risk factors for depression and anxiety in immigrant populations. We aimed to investigate whether parental income mobility patterns during childhood are associated with the risk of depression/anxiety during adolescence and young adulthood among non-immigrants and second-generation immigrants, and whether the association differs by immigrants' region of origin.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Swedish nationwide data on 1,194,015 non-immigrants and 315,793 second-generation immigrants who turned the age of 15 between 2001 and 2020 were used. Income mobility patterns were identified using group-based trajectory modeling based on annual parental income data when the study individuals were aged 0-14. Depression/anxiety was assessed using the National Patient Register (inpatient and outpatient) when the study individuals were aged 15-25. Cox proportional hazard models were used to examine the association between income mobility and depression/anxiety by immigrant status and region of origin.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Five income mobility patterns were identified. Persistent low income was more common among second-generation immigrants than non-immigrants (32.2% versus 12.2%). Compared with persistent high income, persistent low income and downward mobility were associated with higher hazards of depression/anxiety in most groups. Associations were generally weaker among second-generation immigrants, particularly in those from the Middle East or North Africa (MENA). For persistent low income, adjusted hazard ratios (95% Cis) were 2.35 (2.27-2.43) and 2.23 (2.17-2.29) among non-immigrant males and females, versus 1.28 (0.98-1.66) and 1.29 (1.05-1.58) among their MENA counterparts. Among most second-generation immigrant groups, elevated hazards associated with persistent low income were attenuated or absent with upward low-middle mobility.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The association between childhood economic disadvantage and later depression/anxiety varied by immigrant background, with weaker relative risks among second-generation immigrants from MENA. Upward mobility from low to middle income was associated with attenuated risk compared to persistent low income and downward mobility among most second-generation immigrant groups, suggesting that a change of childhood economic circumstances may be relevant to later mental health.

items.title: Prevalence of frailty and associated factors among aging residents with chronic schizophrenia in Taiwanese psychiatric nursing home: a cross-sectional study.
items.authors: Liu TT, Liao SJ, Hsieh CJ.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Frailty is a critical geriatric syndrome reflecting health vulnerability, yet research among residents with chronic schizophrenia remains limited. This study investigated the prevalence and associated factors of frailty in a psychiatric nursing home.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 155 participants from a psychiatric nursing home. Assessment tools included the Frailty Scale, BSRS-5, PANSS, and Barthel Index (ADL/IADL). Data were analyzed using t-tests, Pearson correlation, and multivariable logistic regression.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The prevalence of frailty was 55.5% (86/155). Multivariable logistic regression revealed that female gender (Model 1: adjusted OR = 4.39, 95% CI = 1.92-10.04; Model 2: adjusted OR = 4.33, 95% CI = 1.90-9.85; both p < 0.001) and higher psychological distress (BSRS scores; Model 1: adjusted OR = 1.94, 95% CI = 1.35-2.79; Model 2: adjusted OR = 2.01, 95% CI = 1.42-2.85; both p < 0.001) were significant independent associated with of increased frailty odds. Although the frail group exhibited significantly more severe psychiatric symptoms across all PANSS subscales (all p < 0.01), no significant differences were found in ADL or IADL scores between the two groups.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: These findings suggest that frailty represents a multidimensional vulnerability that co-occurs with psychiatric symptoms alongside preserved functional independence. Routine integration of frailty screening into psychiatric assessments is recommended to inform interdisciplinary care strategies.

items.title: Alcohol as a reported frequent problem and sociodemographic correlates in a Waorani community in the Ecuadorian Amazon: a community-based cross-sectional census study.
items.authors: Zambrano-Villacres R, Quishpi-Choto FR, Quishpi-Contento EG, Cagua-Ordoñez J, Andrade-Mejia N, Simancas-Racines D.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Alcohol-related concerns among Indigenous populations should be interpreted within their specific social, territorial, and historical contexts. Quantitative evidence from Waorani communities in the Ecuadorian Amazon remains limited. This study estimated the proportion of census records in which alcohol was identified as a frequent problem and examined associated sociodemographic characteristics in the Nuevo Amanecer Waorani community.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We conducted a community-based cross-sectional secondary analysis of 125 individual census records from Nuevo Amanecer, Shell Parish, Pastaza Province, Ecuador. The primary outcome was derived from the census item "frequent problem" and was classified as positive when alcohol was selected. Crude and adjusted prevalence ratios (cPRs and aPRs) were estimated using Poisson regression with a log link and HC3 robust sandwich variance. The primary adjusted model included sex, age group, and partnership status. Sensitivity analyses were restricted to adults aged ≥18 years and additionally evaluated educational attainment.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Alcohol was selected as the frequent problem in 81 of 125 census records (64.8%, 95% CI 56.1-72.6). The primary complete-case model included 123 records. Male sex was associated with a higher prevalence of the outcome (aPR 1.31; 95% CI 1.03-1.67). Compared with individuals aged <18 years, higher adjusted prevalence ratios were observed for ages 18-24 years (aPR 2.64; 95% CI 1.58-4.42), 25-34 years (aPR 2.64; 95% CI 1.57-4.42), and ≥45 years (aPR 2.11; 95% CI 1.16-3.83). Stable partnership status showed a more modest association (aPR 1.30; 95% CI 1.00-1.68). In the adult-only analysis ( n  = 80), the association with male sex persisted (aPR 1.24; 95% CI 1.01-1.53), whereas the age pattern changed and the estimate for stable partnership attenuated (aPR 1.21; 95% CI 0.97-1.51).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Alcohol was selected as the frequent problem in nearly two-thirds of census records in this Waorani community. Male sex was the most consistent sociodemographic correlate across analyses, whereas age and partnership associations were more sensitive to the analytical population. These findings should not be interpreted as estimates of individual alcohol consumption, hazardous drinking, or alcohol use disorder. Further research should incorporate culturally and linguistically appropriate, validated alcohol-specific measures, respondent and household identifiers, and longitudinal or mixed-methods approaches developed in collaboration with Waorani leadership.

items.title: Neural and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety: Widespread brain network alterations, increased control costs, and visuospatial processing deficits.
items.authors: Manjunath M, Stamoulis C.

sections.text: This study investigated the neural substrates and cognitive correlates of adolescent anxiety, which are currently incompletely understood, in N = 3,499 youth with median (IQR) age 12.0 (1.1) years (~51.0% females), from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Study. Resting-state fMRI, structural MRI, anxiety (scores and related disorder diagnoses), and neurocognitive data were analyzed. Mixed-effects regression models were used to examine associations between anxiety, brain characteristics (topological and morphometric properties, and regulatory (control) costs of intrinsic network dynamics), and cognitive outcomes. Females, older youth, and those with more parental mental health problems had higher anxiety (β = 0.04-1.15, 95% CI = [0.01, 2.18]). Higher resting-state connectivity and/or centrality (network importance) of the cerebellum, amygdala, and thalamus, and higher cerebellum-basal-ganglia-thalamus control costs were associated with higher anxiety (β = 0.04-0.08, 95% CI = [0.01, 0.11]). In contrast, temporoparietal and frontoparietal network efficiency and resilience (robustness) were protective for social and/or generalized anxiety disorders (adjusted odds ratio (aOR) = 0.72-0.80, 95% CI = [0.62, 0.98]). Higher cortical thickness and/or volume of the superior temporal gyrus, pars opercularis, precentral gyrus, and putamen were associated with higher odds of generalized or social anxiety disorder (aOR = 1.28-1.44, 95% CI = [1.07, 1.78]). Finally, anxiety was associated with lower response accuracy in the Little Man Task (β = -0.05, 95% CI = [-0.09, -0.01]), and attenuated positive brain-task performance associations. These findings suggest that adolescent anxiety is associated with widespread brain alterations, especially in the cerebellum-basal ganglia-thalamus network, while the organization of frontoparietal and temporoparietal networks, which play as key role in emotion regulation and social function, is protective for anxiety disorders. It is also associated with lower visuospatial processing and alterations in the networks that support it.

items.title: Effects of mindfulness-based childbirth preparation education on psychosocial outcomes in pregnancy: a randomized controlled trial.
items.authors: Ocak S, Yılmaz T.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Mindfulness-based interventions have been increasingly integrated into antenatal education programs to improve maternal psychosocial well-being. However, evidence regarding their effects on perceived stress, depressive symptoms, childbirth self-efficacy, and postpartum post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) remains limited and inconsistent. This study aimed to evaluate the effects of Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education (MBCPE) on psychosocial outcomes in primiparous pregnant women.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study was designed as a prospective, randomized controlled trial. The study was completed with 74 pregnant women, including 36 participants in the intervention group and 38 participants in the control group. The intervention group received Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education over eight weeks, while the control group received Information-Based Childbirth Preparation Education over four weeks. Outcome measures included the Perceived Stress Scale, Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, childbirth self-efficacy, and postpartum PTSD symptoms. Statistical analyses were conducted to compare group differences, with significance set at p < 0.05.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A statistically significant difference was found between the intervention and control groups in terms of Perceived Stress Scale and Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale mean scores (p < 0.05), indicating lower stress and depressive symptoms in the intervention group. However, no significant differences were observed between groups in childbirth self-efficacy or postpartum PTSD symptoms assessed at the fourth postpartum week (p > 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Mindfulness-Based Childbirth Preparation Education appears to be effective in reducing perceived stress and depressive symptoms during pregnancy and the postpartum period. items.title: Mapping Brain-Computer Interface Research in Depression (1995-2026): A Bibliometric Analysis.
items.authors: Jiang Y, Duan X.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as promising tools for neuromodulation and emotion regulation in depression. This study aimed to systematically map the global research landscape, thematic evolution, and emerging trends of BCI applications in depressive disorders through bibliometric analysis.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Data were retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection and analyzed using the R package bibliometrix, VOSviewer, and CiteSpace. Publication trends, country and institutional contributions, journal impact, author influence, and keyword-based clustering and burst analysis were comprehensively evaluated.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 239 publications authored by 1284 researchers from 239 institutions across 39 countries were identified. The United States and China had the highest publication outputs, while the United Kingdom showed high citation impact. Laureate Institute for Brain Research was the most productive institution and showed the strongest institutional collaboration, while NeuroImage: Clinical showed the highest journal h-index. Masaya Misaki was the leading author according to publication and citation indicators. Keyword analysis identified six major thematic clusters involving neurophysiological and cognitive features, EEG asymmetry and affective regulation, clinical neurofeedback, connectivity and self-regulation, fMRI-based emotion regulation, and psychiatric symptom/network correlates. "Emotion" showed the strongest keyword burst, while recent bursts in "real-time fMRI neurofeedback," "prefrontal cortex," and "emotion regulation" indicated increasing research attention to circuit-level regulation.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The field has evolved from EEG-based characterization toward network-level and real-time neurofeedback research. These findings identify emerging research directions while highlighting the need for further methodological standardization and clinical validation.

items.title: Nurturing Resilient Minds in Nursing Students: Purpose in Life, Resilience, and Personality-Based Substance Use Risk-A Descriptive Correlational Study.
items.authors: Elfar MNA, Mohamed HMM, Allam SME, Almegewly WH, Baazeem M, Elhapashy HMM, Khedr MA.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Nursing students face sustained academic and clinical stressors that may affect mental health and personality-based substance use vulnerability. Evidence remains limited in Saudi and other Middle Eastern nursing-student populations on whether purpose in life and resilience relate differently to the four substance use risk profile scale (SURPS) personality profiles. This distinction is relevant to profile-specific prevention and student-support services. The study examined relationships among a study-specific modified Purpose in Life (PIL) score, resilience, and the four SURPS profiles and explored associations with demographic characteristics.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We conducted a descriptive correlational study with 915 undergraduate nursing students at a university in Saudi Arabia using an online English-language survey. The PIL test was administered in a study-specific 20-item, 5-point online response format rather than the conventional 7-point semantic-differential format; consequently, the resulting PIL score was treated as a modified within-sample measure and not as psychometrically equivalent to the conventional PIL. SURPS was scored as four separate personality profiles with the positively worded hopelessness items reverse-scored, and CD-RISC-25 responses were recoded to the standard 0-4 metric before summation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Mean scores were 60.55 ± 19.94 for the study-specific modified PIL, 16.32 ± 4.49 for hopelessness, 13.06 ± 3.88 for anxiety sensitivity, 12.56 ± 3.75 for impulsivity, 15.36 ± 4.49 for sensation seeking, and 54.28 ± 24.60 for resilience. The modified PIL score correlated negatively with hopelessness (r = -0.763) and positively with resilience (r = 0.737); resilience correlated negatively with hopelessness (r = -0.770) and positively with anxiety sensitivity, impulsivity, and sensation seeking (r = 0.688, 0.612, and 0.683, respectively; all p < 0.001). Male students had slightly higher impulsivity and sensation-seeking scores, while age and academic-level differences were nonsignificant. Demographic models explained very little variance (R^2 = 0.006-0.012).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Corrected SURPS scoring revealed a profile-specific pattern, but the large correlations and the use of a nonvalidated 5-point PIL response format require cautious interpretation. Hopelessness was strongly inversely associated with the modified PIL score and resilience, whereas anxiety sensitivity, impulsivity, and sensation seeking showed positive associations whose substantive meaning cannot be separated from possible construct overlap or shared-method effects in this cross-sectional self-report dataset. The findings support separate SURPS-profile interpretation rather than an aggregate score, while replication using the conventional PIL format, culturally validated instruments, direct behavioral outcomes, and formal construct-validity testing is needed before stronger clinical inferences are made.

items.title: Validation of the EQ-5D-5L Shona version for screening anxiety and depression in people living with HIV/AIDS.
items.authors: Dambi JM, Purba FD, Shava BK, Doyce SR, Tunduwani T, Hove AR, Chibanda D, Pickard AS, Domingue BW.
items.journal: Health and quality of life outcomes

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Anxiety and depression commonly co-occur among people living with HIV (PLHIV), creating a need for brief tools that can support routine mental health screening. This study evaluated the screening performance, construct validity, and test-retest reliability of the Shona EQ-5D-5L.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study, 611 PLHIV were recruited in Harare, Zimbabwe. The screening performance of the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression item was evaluated against clinician diagnosis and against commonly used screening tools: the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) for depression, the Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) for anxiety, and the Shona Symptoms Questionnaire-14 (SSQ-14) for comorbid anxiety/depression. Sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) were calculated. Construct validity was assessed using correlations between EQ-5D-5L scores and PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SSQ-14 scores. Test-retest reliability was assessed using the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Using a cut-off of ≥ 2, the EQ-5D-5L anxiety/depression item showed acceptable screening performance against clinician diagnosis for anxiety (sensitivity 64.6%, specificity 67.8%, AUROC 0.72), depression (sensitivity 64.1%, specificity 65.8%, AUROC 0.71), and comorbid anxiety/depression (sensitivity 65.8%, specificity 66.3%, AUROC 0.71). The EQ-5D-5L showed similar overall performance to the GAD-7 and PHQ-9 for anxiety and depression screening, respectively, while the SSQ-14 performed slightly better for comorbid anxiety/depression screening. EQ-5D-5L scores were negatively correlated with SSQ-14, GAD-7, and PHQ-9 scores, supporting construct validity. Over two weeks, the EQ-5D-5L showed acceptable stability, with an ICC of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.70; 0.84) for the utility score and 0.73 (95% CI: 0.63; 0.80) for the visual analogue scale (VAS).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The Shona EQ-5D-5L showed acceptable screening performance for anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety/depression among PLHIV, while also providing broader health-related quality-of-life information. These findings support its use as a brief screening and triage tool in routine care and research, alongside rather than in place of condition-specific instruments and clinician assessment.

items.title: Extended-release guanfacine overdose in a pediatric emergency department: a systematic review and a 10-year retrospective chart review.
items.authors: Mohammed O, Chu C, Shah D, Song N, Gamage I, Carciumaru R, Chauhan R, Kam AJ.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To characterize clinical presentations, management strategies and outcomes associated with extended-release guanfacine (ER guanfacine) overdose in pediatric patients presenting to a tertiary care pediatric emergency department (ED) supplemented with a systematic review of published pediatric cases.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A retrospective chart review included patients aged 0 to 18 years presenting with guanfacine overdose to a tertiary pediatric ED between August 2013 and July 2023. Data were extracted on demographics, cause of overdose, clinical features, management and outcomes. Concurrently, a systematic review using the population, exposure, and outcome approach searched MEDLINE and Embase (1974-November 2025) to consolidate existing case-report evidence on emergent management of guanfacine overdose in pediatric patients.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Ten studies met inclusion criteria, describing eleven pediatric cases, mostly accidental with ingestions in younger children, with bradycardia and hypotension reported frequently.Management was supportive; naloxone produced variable benefit, and when used no deaths occurred. For the retrospective cohort, (n = 15; median age 14), 73% involved intentional ingestions and were frequently associated with psychiatric comorbidities. Bradycardia and hypotension were nearly universal; with some patients demonstrating transient hypertension. Treatment included intravenous fluids (87%) and atropine for symptomatic bradycardia (20%). Three patients required pediatric intensive care unit admission; none received naloxone. All patients recovered fully without mortality.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: ER guanfacine overdose most commonly affects adolescents with underlying mental health conditions and presents with clinically significant cardiovascular depression. Management is supportive, emphasizing fluid resuscitation and cardiac monitoring. Findings support the need for standardized ED care pathways and integrated mental-health interventions.

items.title: Development and Internal Validation of a Risk Prediction Model for Clozapine-Induced Gastrointestinal Hypomotility: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study.
items.authors: Tian FJ, Zhang Y, Tian JK, Cui HL, Song P.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To develop and internally validate a prediction model for a first episode of clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) in clozapine-treated psychiatric inpatients.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this single-center retrospective cohort study, 1,426 adults with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or bipolar disorder who had received clozapine for at least 4 weeks and were admitted to the Department of Psychiatry of Beijing United Family Rehabilitation Hospital between January 2019 and December 2025 were included. The index date was defined as the date of the current psychiatric admission, and all predictors were measured at or before that date. The outcome was a first CIGH event within 90 days, defined as paralytic ileus or intestinal obstruction, severe constipation requiring pharmacological intervention, or fecal impaction. Predictors were selected using LASSO regression, and the model was constructed with multivariable logistic regression. Performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), the calibration curve and decision curve analysis, and internal validation used 1,000 bootstrap resamples. Static and interactive (Shiny) nomograms were developed.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: CIGH occurred in 356 of 1,426 patients (24.96%). Six predictors were retained: age ≥60 years (OR 1.469, 95% CI 1.031-2.094), BMI <24 kg/m^2 (OR 1.699, 95% CI 1.099-2.628), daily clozapine dose ≥300 mg (OR 2.276, 95% CI 1.531-3.384), clozapine treatment duration ≥5 years (OR 2.309, 95% CI 1.431-3.725), concomitant use of trihexyphenidyl (OR 3.322, 95% CI 2.291-4.818) and predominantly bedridden status (OR 2.608, 95% CI 1.817-3.744). Discrimination was moderate (AUC 0.731, 95% CI 0.694-0.768; bootstrap-corrected AUC 0.718), calibration was acceptable, and decision curve analysis indicated net benefit across threshold probabilities of 15%-70%.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This internally validated model provides a non-invasive aid for stratifying 90-day CIGH risk in clozapine-treated psychiatric inpatients and for structuring gastrointestinal monitoring. External validation and prospective evaluation of clinical utility are required before routine implementation.

items.title: Differences in associations between coping styles and depressive symptoms across pandemic-related periods among university students with subthreshold depressive symptoms: a serial cross-sectional study.
items.authors: Miyake Y, Yoshino A, Okamoto Y.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic has significantly affected the mental health of university students. However, differences in mental health and coping styles across pandemic-related periods remain insufficiently understood. Although coping styles have been associated with depressive symptoms, it remains unclear whether these associations differ across pandemic-related periods among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms, a high-risk group for clinical depression. This study examined differences in depressive symptoms, disordered eating behaviors, and coping styles across pandemic-related periods, with a particular focus on the association between coping styles and depressive symptoms among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This serial cross-sectional study included 24,438 Japanese university students who were assessed during the pandemic (2021-2022), transition (2023), and post-pandemic (2024-2025) periods. Depressive symptoms, disordered eating behaviors, and coping styles were assessed using the Beck Depression Inventory-II (BDI-II), Eating Attitudes Test-26 (EAT-26), Bulimic Inventory Test, Edinburgh (BITE), and Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations (CISS). Associations between coping styles and depressive symptoms among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms were examined using partial correlation and multiple regression analyses.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The BDI-II and BITE scores were lower during the transition and post-pandemic periods than during the pandemic period. The EAT-26 scores showed a significant interaction between period and sex. The CISS-T scores were lower during the pandemic than during the transition and post-pandemic periods, whereas the CISS-A scores were higher in the post-pandemic period. Among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms, CISS-E scores were positively correlated with depressive symptoms across all periods, whereas the associations involving CISS-T scores differed across periods.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Depressive symptoms and coping styles among university students differed across the pandemic-related periods. Among students with subthreshold depressive symptoms, emotion-oriented coping showed a consistent association with depressive symptoms, whereas associations involving task-oriented coping differed across periods. These findings suggest that the association between coping styles and depressive symptoms may differ according to environmental conditions. Considering the environmental context may be important when developing preventive and supportive interventions for students' mental health.

items.title: Clinical improvement despite rising anti-streptococcal antibody titers during adjunctive bacteriophage therapy in refractory PANDAS: a hypothesis-generating case report.
items.authors: Recordare A, Dadiani M, Nizharadze D, Nadareishvili L, Pirozzolo G, Palumbo R, Girotto C, Mezzapelle G, Kutateladze M.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Pediatric Autoimmune Neuropsychiatric Disorders Associated with Streptococcal infections (PANDAS) are characterized by the abrupt onset of anxiety, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, tics, and other neuropsychiatric manifestations associated with Group A Streptococcus exposure. Although antimicrobial and immunomodulatory therapies are widely employed, many patients experience persistent or relapsing symptoms despite prolonged treatment. Bacteriophage therapy has not previously been reported in PANDAS and represents an experimental, pathogen-directed therapeutic approach.

sections.heading: Case presentation
sections.text: We report the case of an 11-year-old girl with severe refractory PANDAS characterized by obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety, motor and vocal tics, emotional dysregulation, insomnia, agitation, and marked functional impairment, including school refusal. The diagnosis was supported by elevated antistreptococcal serology. The patient received several escalating interventions, including intramuscular benzathine penicillin, azithromycin, plasma exchange, intravenous immunoglobulins, psychotherapy, and aripiprazole. A clinical improvement was initially observed after penicillin administration, although the benefit was incomplete and transient. No active streptococcal isolate was available for phage susceptibility testing. On the basis of repeated antibiotic responsiveness, empirical anti-streptococcal bacteriophage therapy was initiated using Pyo Bacteriophages (Eliava biopreparation), administered twice daily for three 15-day cycles as add-on therapy, while antibiotics were maintained.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Clinical sustained improvement became evident approximately six days after initiation of bacteriophage therapy, mirroring the latency previously observed after penicillin, and was followed by sustained clinical stabilization. No adverse events were reported. Serial serological evaluation demonstrated a paradoxical increase in ASO and anti-DNase titres despite continuous neurological and psychiatric improvement.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This case suggests that bacteriophage therapy may represent a plausible pathogen-directed strategy in selected patients with refractory PANDAS, particularly when a reproducible clinical response to anti-streptococcal antibiotics suggests persistent microbial involvement. items.title: The Traumatic Event in the Age of PTSD: Psychoanalysis, Neurology, and Literature.
items.authors: Bar-Haim S.
items.journal: Journal of the history of the behavioral sciences

sections.text: The DSM-III (1980) defined a traumatic event as a horrific event that is "outside the range of usual human experience," such as genocide, war, a terror attack, or rape. However, by the publication of the DSM-IV in 1994, there was a substantial expansion of the criteria for what a traumatic event could be, and who could be considered a victim of such an event. In the first decades of the 21st century, the discourse of trauma is ubiquitous in medical and cultural domains alike. Still, the traumatic event itself lost much of its currency, and trauma as such changed much of its meaning. This article documents the process by which this epistemological shift unfolded. The first part of the article presents the pedagogical intervention of literary scholar Shoshana Felman in 1984, in which she deliberately aimed to trigger highly emotional reactions in students by exposing them to recorded testimonies of Holocaust survivors. Emotional triggering stands, she believed, at the core of meaningful teaching of trauma in history. Felman was also a major figure in the second phase presented here, which took place in the mid-1990s, with the fruitful and somewhat surprising collaboration between neurologically oriented clinicians such as the psychiatrists Bessel van der Kolk and Onno van der Hart the literary scholar Cathy Caruth and Felman. This collaboration contributed to the promotion of a new understanding of trauma in which triggers and flashbacks turned into the two main focal concepts in trauma discourse-and for PTSD to be popularized far beyond medical circles and academia, entering wider public domains and popular culture. This was the moment-as will be discussed in the last part of this piece-that a new "trigger culture" emerged (Ziv and Bar-Haim, 2024). The notion that traumatic events from the past have long-lasting and harmful effects on one's life has turned into an ongoing effort by individuals and the public to mitigate potential traumatic triggers in an unknown future.

items.title: Trends in and program characteristics associated with pre-exposure prophylaxis availability among opioid treatment facilities in the United States.
items.authors: Figgatt MC, Jaiswal J, Alnashri Y, Rosen JG, Rich JD, Green TC.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To examine the prevalence and settings of PrEP availability at opioid use treatment facilities in the United States.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We examined PrEP trends from 2021 to 2024 using the National Substance Use and Mental Health Services Survey. Using multivariable logistic regression models, we calculated odds ratios (OR) and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) to examine associations between facility characteristics and PrEP prescribing in 2024.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 13,755 substance use treatment facilities in 2021; 14,201 in 2022; 12,892 in 2023; and 13,875 in 2024 were included. The percentage of facilities offering PrEP increased from 6.03% in 2021 to 10.62% in 2024 ( p  < 0.01) nationwide. Despite comprising over 90% of facilities, outpatient (8.57%) and residential (14.26%) facilities had lower PrEP availability than inpatient facilities (23.19%). Facilities with methadone and buprenorphine had higher odds of PrEP availability (methadone OR = 7.52, 95% CI = 5.34, 10.59; buprenorphine only OR = 10.09, 95% CI = 7.53, 13.52) compared to those without these treatments. Facilities offering programs specific to people living with HIV (OR = 2.32, 95% CI = 1.83, 2.94) and those identifying as LGBTQ+ (OR = 1.75, 95% CI = 1.35, 2.27) were more likely to offer PrEP.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Despite the high number of people served in outpatient and residential facilities, PrEP access continues to remain low.

items.title: Psychedelics in neurosurgery: Potential utility in prevention, perioperative care, pain management, and neurorehabilitation.
items.authors: Garcia-Bitar A, Castañeda EJ, Buenrostro-Rangel JR, Vázquez-Flores AK, Santibañez-Patiño PD, Moreno-Jiménez S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Neurosurgical patients carry a high and frequently undertreated burden of psychological suffering, acute and chronic pain, and neurological deficits amenable to recovery. The resurgence of psychedelic research has produced relevant evidence in adjacent fields, but its applicability to neurosurgery has not been systematized. This review synthesizes that evidence across prevention, perioperative care, pain management, and neurorehabilitation, and delineates the safety considerations specific to neurosurgery.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Narrative review structured around a population, intervention, comparator, outcome, and time question, covering 2020-2026. The classic serotonergic psychedelics (psilocybin, lysergic acid diethylamide [LSD], N,N-dimethyltryptamine, ayahuasca, 5-methoxy-N,N-dimethyltryptamine, and mescaline), the iboga alkaloid ibogaine, the entactogen 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine, and the dissociatives ketamine and esketamine were examined. Randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and high-quality mechanistic studies were prioritized.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: No trial has administered these agents in neurosurgical cohorts, so all evidence is indirect. Psilocybin- assisted therapy produces substantial, durable reductions in cancer-related depression, anxiety, and existential distress. LSD is anxiolytic; parenteral tryptamines act rapidly in depression; ibogaine improved disability, post- traumatic stress, and cognition after traumatic brain injury but carries arrhythmia risk. Perioperative ketamine and esketamine show antidepressant and opioid-sparing effects. Classic psychedelics promote neuroplasticity and are neuroprotective in preclinical models.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: A biologically plausible basis exists for exploring these agents in neurosurgery, but direct evidence is absent and translation is constrained by the seizure threshold, hemodynamic and cerebrovascular effects, perioperative serotonergic interactions, and the need for structured psychological support. Perioperative esketamine and psilocybin for neuro-oncological distress are the most feasible starting points. Purpose-designed neurosurgical trials are required.

items.title: Key determinants of antiretroviral therapy adherence among Thai youth living with HIV: the mediating role of HIV self-management behaviors.
items.authors: Saenjun P, Prasopkittikun T, Vongsirimas N, Maneesriwongul W, Mekmullica J, Voss JG.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Thai youth living with HIV (YLHIV) aged 15-24 demonstrate poorer antiretroviral therapy (ART) adherence than adults; however, factors associated with self-management behaviors and adherence remain insufficiently understood. This study examined psychosocial, clinical, and relational factors associated with HIV self-management behaviors and ART adherence.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional study recruited 210 participants (minimum 10 participants per estimated parameter), aged 15-24, from six tertiary hospitals in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region between May 1 and November 30, 2024. Participants completed self-administered questionnaires during routine clinic visits. Mediation analysis examined associations of depressive symptoms, comorbidities, family support, peer support, perceived public stigma, and patient-healthcare provider relationship with ART adherence (30-day Visual Analog Scale; good adherence ≥ 95%) through HIV self-management behaviors, adjusting for education, HIV disclosure status, and ART duration.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Participants had a mean age of 21.65 years (SD = 2.15) with 90% aged between 19 and 24 years; 74.8% were male. The model explained 69.8% of the variance in ART adherence. HIV self-management behaviors were positively associated with adherence (β_z = 0.237, p < 0.01). Depressive symptoms (β_z = - 0.210, p < 0.01), comorbidities (β_z = - 0.129, p < 0.05), and perceived public stigma (β_z = - 0.224, p < 0.01) were negatively associated with HIV self-management behaviors, while family support (β_z = 0.148, p < 0.05), and patient-healthcare provider relationship (βz = 0.153, p < 0.05) were positively associated. Depressive symptoms (β_z = - 0.196, p < 0.01), comorbidities (β_z = - 0.111, p < 0.05), and perceived public stigma (β_z = - 0.169, p < 0.05) were negatively associated with ART adherence, while family support (β_z = 0.155, p < 0.01) and patient-healthcare provider relationship (β_z = 0.128, p < 0.05) were positively associated. All associations, except comorbidities, were partially mediated by HIV self-management behaviors. Peer support was not significantly associated with either outcome.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Among Thai YLHIV receiving ART care in tertiary hospitals in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region, predominantly older adolescents and young adults, ART adherence was associated with psychosocial, relational, and clinical factors, with significant indirect associations observed through HIV self-management behaviors. Findings support multi-component, developmentally appropriate strategies integrating mental health screening, stigma reduction, family engagement, youth-sensitive communication, and coordinated management of comorbid conditions. Strengthening HIV self-management capacity represents an important target for comprehensive adherence support among this population.

items.title: The molecular and neurochemical basis of altered intrinsic neural timescales in major depressive disorder: a multimodal imaging-transcriptomic investigation of esketamine and sertraline treatment.
items.authors: Liu X, He Y, Li L, Hu Z, Li H, Wu L, Zhang L, Su Z, Liu H, Wu G, Peng D.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is characterized by dysfunction in higher-order cortical regions involved in emotional and cognitive processes; however, its neurobiological basis remains unclear. Pharmacological treatments, including esketamine and sertraline, produce rapid antidepressant effects. We investigated the local intrinsic neural dynamics underlying these antidepressant effects using intrinsic neural timescales (INT), which measure the duration and capacity of information integration in localized brain regions.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 57 healthy controls and 41 patients with MDD were included. All patients with MDD received six intravenous infusions of esketamine (0.25 mg/kg) and two weeks of sertraline treatment. All participants underwent resting-state fMRI to quantify INT alterations at the voxel and brain network levels, followed by spatial correlation analyses linking autocorrelation metrics of INT signals to transcriptomic data from the Allen Human Brain Atlas and PET-derived neurotransmitter receptor maps. The spatial correlation between PLS2 scores and case-control t-statistic maps did not pass rigorous spin permutation testing (r = 0.484, p = 0.068) and did not meet the conventional significance threshold of 0.05. Accordingly, all subsequent enrichment analyses based on PLS2 results are presented as exploratory preliminary observations for hypothesis generation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Compared with healthy controls, patients with MDD exhibited significantly elevated INT levels in the left and right precuneus. Following treatment, patients with MDD showed significantly increased INT in the left occipital midline region and left calcarine cortex. At the brain network level, INT levels were significantly reduced in the default mode network (DMN) in patients with MDD compared with healthy controls. Compared with the pre-treatment state, the cerebellar network (CN) showed significantly elevated INT levels after treatment. Partial least squares regression analysis suggested potential associations between INT alterations and spatial gene expression gradients particularly those associated with immune responses, hormonal regulation, neutrophils, regulatory T cells, and glutamatergic synapses. Cell-type enrichment analysis identified excitatory and inhibitory neurons as key cellular contributors. Alterations in INT also correlated with cortical 5-HT1b and NAT receptor density, suggesting a role for inhibitory neurotransmission in temporal integration deficits.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study advances understanding of treatment-related brain abnormalities in patients with MDD from the perspective of local neural dynamics. These findings support a multiscale pathophysiological framework involving brain connectivity dynamics, molecular architecture, and neurochemical regulation in MDD.

items.title: The effect of grief counseling on depression and post-traumatic stress disorder in women following perinatal deaths.
items.authors: Nournorouzi L, Hakimi S, Esmaeilpour K, Najmi LA, Nourizadeh R.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Fetal or neonatal death is a tragic event that frequently leads to the mother experiencing grief, as well as the development of depression and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). The present study aimed to determine the impact of grief counseling on depression and PTSD in women following perinatal deaths.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This experimental study was conducted on 56 women who had experienced perinatal deaths within the previous 1-3 months in Tabriz, Iran. Participants were randomly assigned to either the intervention or control group based on the type of perinatal loss (stillbirth or neonatal death). For the intervention group, grief counseling was provided individually in three sessions, one per week, lasting 45-60 min. Data collection tools included a demographic and obstetric questionnaire, the Edinburgh Depression Scale, and the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5). Data analysis was performed using SPSS version 24. ANCOVA was employed to compare depression and PTSD ratings pre- and post-intervention while adjusting for confounding variables.

sections.heading: Findings
sections.text: The two groups had no significant demographic differences (p > 0.05). One month after the intervention, the mean depression score in the intervention group was significantly lower than in the control group (adjusted mean difference = - 2, 95% confidence interval: - 3.2 to - 0.8, p = 0.01). However, the mean PTSD score did not differ significantly between the two groups (adjusted mean difference = - 1.5, 95% confidence interval: - 7.5 to 4.4, p = 0.59).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Grief counseling after fetal or neonatal loss led to a reduction in depression, but no significant effect on PTSD symptoms was observed with this intervention. It is recommended to use other counseling approaches and assess their effectiveness for PTSD following perinatal deaths.

items.title: An exploratory study of relationships between the executive functions and spatiotemporal control in a complex motor task: the spatial tapping task.
items.authors: Dione M, Alhaddad G, Longcamp M, Delevoye-Turrell Y.

sections.text: Executive functions (EFs) are cognitive processes enabling planning, control, and regulation of behavior. A variety of tasks have been developed to evaluate EFs, from complex reasoning to simpler inhibition tasks, reflecting the diversity of symptoms observed in patients with executive deficits. Recent research has emphasized their unity, proposing three core functions, working memory, inhibition, and switching, that share resources and combine to enable complex tasks. Yet, no single task captures both the unity and diversity of EFs, limiting the development of a unified framework and a balanced assessment. To address this gap, we designed the spatial tapping task, a timing paradigm combining finger tapping and circle drawing. Finger tapping requires working memory for explicit timing control, whereas circle drawing requires anticipatory control akin to switching to control movement trajectory, enabling implicit timing control. Participants produce taps along a circular trajectory with the tempo increasing progressively. A slow tempo favors discrete movements with long pauses between taps, whereas a fast tempo promotes continuous motion. Previous analyses supported a change in timing control mode with increasing tempo. Here, we explored the hypothesis that EFs are engaged accordingly: working memory in the slow/discrete phase, switching in the fast/continuous phase, and inhibition in the intermediate phase, where demands for continuous motion increase. In two studies combined into a single dataset, we compared scores with those from neuropsychological tests using correlations. We found that timing accuracy in the slow/discrete phase was associated with working memory, spatial accuracy in the fast/continuous phase with switching, and longer contact time in the intermediate phase with inhibition. We also explored whether performance was consistent with the EF deficits described in the literature, and the potential contribution of motor output, reporting scores obtained across populations with executive deficits (aging and dementia), combined executive and motor impairments (schizophrenia), and motor expertise (biscriptual writers), along with matched controls. Findings were consistent, although often more specific, and highlighted an important contribution of motor output. Altogether, our results provide initial evidence that the task can be used to investigate EFs, although cognitive, motor, and sensory contributions need to be disentangled to improve its specificity.

Participants produce taps along a circular trajectory with the tempo increasing progressively. items.title: Anxiety Before and After Drug Provocation Testing in Drug Hypersensitivity: Who Remains Anxious Despite a Reassuring Test?
items.authors: Kural RF, Tunakan Dalgıç C, İnan S, Özışık M, Akten S, Okan K, Gumusburun R, Mete Gökmen EN, Sin AZ.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.text: Drug provocation testing (DPT) is the gold standard for diagnosing drug hypersensitivity reactions (DHRs). We assessed the change in anxiety from baseline to one week after DPT and identified which patients remain anxious despite a negative (reassuring) test, alongside correlates of the nocebo response.

sections.heading: Patients and methods
sections.text: In this ambispective (retro-prospective) two-center study, 155 adults with suspected immediate-type DHR underwent single-blind, placebo-controlled DPT. Anxiety was measured with the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) before and one week after testing. Factors associated with baseline anxiety, residual (post-test) anxiety and the nocebo response were examined in the full cohort. For residual anxiety, the post-test BAI score was the primary outcome, and a sensitivity analysis was restricted to DPT-negative patients.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: DPT was negative in 147 patients (94.8%); among 57 tested with the culprit drug, 53 (93.0%) were de-labeled. BAI fell from 15.7±15.0 to 4.8±7.8 (p<0.001; r=0.75). The proportion with at least moderate anxiety (BAI ≥16) decreased from 41.9% to 5.2%. Residual anxiety (BAI ≥8) persisted in 36 patients (23.2%) and was associated with baseline anxiety. Baseline anxiety was associated mainly with a severe index reaction, psychiatric history and low income. Atopy showed an exploratory, baseline-adjusted association with residual anxiety (+3.2 points; p=0.004). A nocebo response occurred in 20.0% of patients. In exploratory multivariable analysis, recurrent prior reactions remained independently associated with this response (low income less consistently), whereas baseline anxiety did not.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In this single-arm study, anxiety fell substantially after DPT and most patients tested with the culprit drug were de-labeled, but a negative result did not reassure everyone. Residual anxiety was associated with elevated baseline anxiety and, less robustly, with atopy; nocebo responses related mainly to recurrent prior reactions. Brief pre-test screening could thus direct targeted psychological support to those least reassured by testing alone.

items.title: Protocol: Research Priorities in Autism and Eating Disorders Research: An Evidence and Gap Map of Primary Studies and Systematic Reviews.
items.authors: Rodriguez L, Gillespie-Smith K, Duffy F, Sharpe H, Nimbley E, Austin A.

sections.text: This is a protocol for a Campbell Evidence and Gap Map (EGM) focused on identifying the number, types and quality of evidence that exists on research priorities identified in Keller et al. (2024) and Nimbley et al. (2024). The specific objectives are to: (1) Identify and map all existing primary studies and systematic reviews (published and unpublished) on the research priorities identified in the body of research on autism and eating disorders. (2) Provide a comprehensive, descriptive overview of the existing research in these research priorities areas by targeted age groups, country, gender, sex, ethnicity, eating disorder diagnosis and autism status (diagnosis or trait) and (3) Determine the type of evidence available in these research priorities identified, as well as ascertain the quality of the evidence of systematic reviews and RCTs. For this purpose, a search strategy will be developed in conjunction with an expert subject librarian and piloted. A systematic search will be carried out using the following platforms and specific databases: Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, Ovid (PsycINFO and Medline(r) All), ProQuest (Applied Social Science and Index Abstracts (ASSIA) and Social Science Database) and Overton. This EGM will consider primary studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses, both published and unpublished, as well as grey literature in English and Spanish. Data extraction will be conducted in duplicate. Data required for AMSTAR 2 (systematic reviews) and the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 1 will be used to evaluate the quality of randomised control trials.

items.title: Educational Burnout and Psychopathology Among School and University Students: A Systematic Review Protocol.
items.authors: Bochniarz KT, Jurek P, Atroszko PA.

sections.text: Educational burnout is increasingly recognized as an important problem among school and university students and has been associated with a range of mental health difficulties. However, existing reviews have largely focused on selected outcomes, particularly depression and anxiety, or on specific student populations, such as medical students, leaving the broader relationship between educational burnout and psychopathology insufficiently synthesized. This protocol outlines a systematic review and meta-analysis examining associations between educational burnout and psychopathology among school and university students, with psychopathology defined in relation to ICD-10 and ICD-11 diagnostic categories and encompassing clinically diagnosed or probable disorders and dimensional psychopathological symptoms. Quantitative studies using validated measures of educational burnout will be identified through searches of Scopus, MEDLINE, ERIC, APA PsycArticles, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses Global, and EBSCO Open Dissertations. Risk of bias will be assessed using the revised JBI critical appraisal tool for cross-sectional studies. Where sufficiently comparable evidence is available, associations will be synthesized using random-effects meta-analysis, with moderator analyses conducted where data permit; otherwise, findings will be synthesized narratively. School and university students will be analyzed separately to account for differences in developmental and educational contexts. By synthesizing evidence across a broad spectrum of psychopathology and different educational contexts, the review aims to clarify the associations between educational burnout and psychopathology and inform future research, measurement practices, and prevention strategies.

items.title: Reflecting on Youth Participation in Mental Health Research: Lessons From the Consell de Joves in Catalonia.
items.authors: Bennett M, Lozano-Sánchez A, Guzmán-Molina C, Jacques-Aviñó C.
items.journal: Health expectations : an international journal of public participation in health care and health policy

sections.text: Participatory approaches in youth and adolescent mental health research are increasingly recognised as important for producing research that is relevant, ethical, and responsive to young people's experiences. However, research remains shaped by adult-centred structures that can limit young people's influence and reproduce inequities in whose knowledge is recognised. This article presents a reflexive account of the development and implementation of the Consell de Joves (CJ), a youth advisory council embedded within a 3-year mental health research project in Catalonia, Spain (2023-2025). The CJ involved young people across study design, development of research instruments, interpretation of findings, and dissemination. Drawing on established frameworks for youth participation, we reflect on five areas of practice: ethics, safeguarding, and power considerations; recruitment and composition; meeting logistics and participation; youth involvement in research design and dissemination; and ongoing reflection and feedback. We examine how principles of meaningful participation were operationalized, including areas of alignment, tensions, and adaptations. The experience highlighted both the possibilities and limitations of youth participation within institutionally constrained research environments. Flexible engagement, attention to psychological safety, and opportunities for meaningful input supported participation and peer exchange. However, structural barriers related to time, travel, socioeconomic circumstances, and institutional schedules constrained participation. Persistent tensions also emerged around adult-youth power relations, representation, remuneration, and the extent of youth influence within an adult-led research structure. Reflecting critically on the CJ illustrates how principles of youth participation can be translated into practice while revealing the structural conditions that may constrain their implementation. We provide two practical resources: a reflective journal of recommendations and a step-by-step roadmap with critical questions to support more equitable youth participation. PATIENT OR PUBLIC CONTRIBUTION: Young people participated in the design, conduct, interpretation and dissemination of the broader mental health research project through the Consell de Joves (Youth Advisory Council). Council members contributed to shaping research questions, refining interview guides and study materials, interpreting research findings, and advising on dissemination strategies and outputs. They also provided feedback on their experiences of participating in the CJ, which informed the research team's ongoing reflection. However, the present manuscript is a retrospective reflective account developed by the research team. CJ members were not involved in the formal analysis or interpretation of the reflective material concerning the council itself, nor in the development or writing of this manuscript. Their contributions to the broader project and feedback on the CJ experience are acknowledged throughout the paper.

items.title: Determinants of psychosocial wellbeing within a year-long youth cycling program.
items.authors: Adamic EM, Wozniak MJ, Dickerson CM, Miller LC, Panther JL, Vanderberg A, Whorton J, Brown CL.
items.journal: Frontiers in sports and active living

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: School-based cycling programs are increasingly being implemented as accessible means to promote overall wellbeing in youth through structured physical activity. As these programs continue to develop, more rigorous research approaches can be used to better understand how these programs impact participant wellbeing outcomes. Here, we sought to examine within-subject trends and identify multivariate predictors of psychosocial wellbeing among youth participating in "Bike Club", a year-long after-school cycling program.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We studied 329 fourth- through eighth-grade students enrolled in Bike Club across 37 schools in Tulsa, Oklahoma. We assessed pre- and post-program psychosocial wellbeing using survey-based scales, and used mixed-effects stepwise linear regression to explore the relationship of individual changes in wellbeing with self-reported physical activity, outdoor time, perceived help with emotions, connection with nature, and bike self-efficacy, along with demographic variables.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Initial paired analysis indicated no significant group-level change in wellbeing between pre- and post-program, despite substantial individual variability (56% of participants reported meaningful changes). Perceived help with emotions and physical activity were most closely associated with wellbeing, followed by modifiable variables like outdoor time and bike self-efficacy and demographic variables like gender, race and ethnicity, and English language learning status. Although the program significantly increased bike self-efficacy and daily outdoor time, it did not appear to significantly relate to the frequency of physical activity or perceived emotional support.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: While school-based cycling programs may support positive youth development with the potential to influence multiple correlates of wellbeing, our findings suggest they may not independently produce consistent mental health improvements when relying on incidental activity exposure alone. Perhaps intentional integration of psychosocial or therapeutic components is needed for cycling programs to support improvement in wellbeing, with longitudinal study designs across multiple timepoints and comparison groups to better isolate program effects while integrating more targeted intervention strategies.

items.title: "It helps calm my mind"-Exploring the Connection of Religion, Spirituality, and Mindfulness in Adolescents With Diabetes.
items.authors: Jengelley DHA, Machuca LA, Baumberger G, Varner-Perez SE, Hannon TS.
items.journal: Global advances in integrative medicine and health

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Adolescents with diabetes participate in daily disease management tasks yet often have underdeveloped coping skills and lack consistent support. The negative emotional impact of diabetes is often associated with poor mental and physical health outcomes. Religious, spiritual, or mindfulness practices may augment coping strategies to support positive diabetes outcomes.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: We examined adolescents' thoughts and beliefs about the relevance of religious, spiritual or mindfulness practices in their diabetes management. We inquired if a mindfulness-based intervention might be of interest as part of comprehensive diabetes education and treatment.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Quantitative surveys-demographic, pediatric quality of life, and spiritual, religious, and personal beliefs-and qualitative interviews were conducted in 18 participants aged 14-18 years old to explore how religious, spiritual, or personal beliefs were perceived to impact coping with prediabetes, type 1, or type 2 diabetes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Health-related quality of life was associated with spirituality, religious, and personal beliefs measured by (r=0.51, p =5.4x10^-10; r=0.61, p =1.01x10^-9). Most participants identified as having a religion, and their impressions of non-religious spiritual practices were varied. For all participants that engaged in spiritual practices (non-religious/religious), they believed these practices were beneficial for their mental health, but did not identify these practices as having an impact on diabetes management. Participants had limited knowledge of or familiarity with mindfulness practices and expressed apprehension when providing input about a potential mindfulness-based group intervention. Despite these concerns, participants voiced that mindfulness could be helpful for dealing with stress.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Additional feasibility and acceptability work is needed to explore complementary therapies, such as mindfulness-based interventions, in adolescents with diabetes.

items.title: Severe neuropsychiatric manifestations in a 17-year-old male with a 20p13 interstitial deletion encompassing CSNK2A1: a case report.
items.authors: Laubach JP, Zeeb D, Weber S, Becker K, Seipelt P.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Microdeletions of 20p13 involving CSNK2A1 have rarely been reported and may be associated with an Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome compatible phenotype. Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome is a rare neurodevelopmental syndrome (OCNDS) caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in CSNK2A1 and is characterized by a broad spectrum of symptoms including developmental delays and intellectual disability.

sections.heading: Case presentation
sections.text: This case report describes a 17-year-old male with de novo interstitial 419 kb 20p13 microdeletion involving the CSNK2A1 gene, which may represent a potential contributor to an OCNDS-compatible phenotype. In addition to rarely reported features such as intrauterine growth restriction or vesicoureteral reflux, there are pronounced psychiatric abnormalities, including a severe depressive episode with psychotic symptoms that has not previously been described in connection with Okur-Chung neurodevelopmental syndrome.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Assuming that the CSNK2A1 deletion represents the potential contributor to the OCNDS-compatible phenotype, this case may expand the phenotypic spectrum of OCNDS and highlights the need for a better understanding of the underlying genetic mechanisms and their contribution to the clinical phenotype.

items.title: Toward an Occupational Justice-Informed Vocational Rehabilitation Framework for Mental Health Service Users in Namibia: A Delphi Study.
items.authors: Chimara M, van Biljon H, Adams F, van Niekerk L.

sections.heading: Introduction and rationale
sections.text: A vocational rehabilitation practice framework is needed to promote shared clinical reasoning among occupational therapists and support consistent, contextually relevant services for mental health service users in Namibia. This study sought expert consensus on foundational components that could guide the future development of such a framework. An occupational justice orientation informed the conceptual framing, viewing vocational rehabilitation as both a therapeutic and advocacy-based process aimed at promoting equitable access to meaningful work.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A modified Delphi method was employed to obtain consensus from a panel of 11 experts on 50 statements derived from three datasets. The process included two Delphi survey rounds, conducted using a 3-point Likert scale via REDCap software. Consensus was defined as 75% or greater agreement on a given item.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Consensus was reached on 38 of the 50 statements (76%). Items endorsed by the panel emphasized foundational strategies, including advancing occupational justice through advocacy for equitable work opportunities, engaging families and employers, applying individualized and client-centered approaches such as place-and-train, and aligning services with national mental health and disability policies. These findings represent areas of shared professional priority rather than a finalized practice framework.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The study demonstrates consensus among experts that vocational rehabilitation practice in Namibia requires attention to both individual work-readiness support and the broader systemic conditions that shape access to meaningful work for service users. The priorities identified offer a critical evidence base that will inform and shape the final phase of developing the vocational rehabilitation framework.

items.title: How to Elicit Thought Disorder During Clinical Interviews: A Practical Guide.
items.authors: Palaniyappan L, Delgaram-Nejad O, Chen EY.

sections.text: The reliable assessment of Formal Thought Disorder (FTD), a collection of observable signs of suspected thinking dysfunction, is the cornerstone of interviewing a person with psychosis. A significant gap persists between the success of reliable assessments reported in published rating scales of FTD and the practical constraints of a clinical interview. Validated rating scales largely focus on operationalized criteria for describing items; the procedural aspects of how to elicit these signs often remain implicit. We synthesize the principles and procedures of FTD assessment embedded in rating scales, translating their design into a framework for routine clinical use. Systematic employment of several manoeuvres can help elicit FTD signs: conversational stimulation, cognitive loading, social modulation, and pointed clarifications to stress-test thought, language and communication processes. items.title: Patients recover while surgeons suffer: a narrative review on surgical ergonomics in laparoscopic surgery.
items.authors: Mohammad Azmi N, Dualim DM, Balaganapathi S, Azman ZAM, Hayati MFM.

sections.heading: Background and objective
sections.text: Laparoscopic surgery offers significant patient benefits but introduces substantial ergonomic challenges, leading to a high prevalence of work-related musculoskeletal disorders, fatigue, and burnout. This narrative review aims to synthesize current evidence on ergonomic risks in laparoscopic surgery, their impact on surgeons' health and performance and potential mitigation strategies.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We conducted a narrative review of relevant literature on PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science and SCOPUS databases using the keywords "surgical ergonomics, laparoscopic surgery, minimally-invasive surgery, robotic surgery, surgeon wellbeing, musculoskeletal disorder, surgeon career longevity" to elucidate this issue.

sections.heading: Key content and findings
sections.text: Ergonomic hazards frequently stem from suboptimal operating room setups, improper table and monitor positioning, "one-size-fits-all" instrument designs and non-neutral postures such as the "mirror image" effect. These factors contribute to physical complaints affecting up to 88% of laparoscopic surgeons, which may compromise surgical precision and patient safety. Assessment tools like the Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) are instrumental in quantifying these physical and cognitive demands. Potential interventions to combat this include targeted ergonomic training such as the Alexander Technique, intraoperative micro-breaks and wearable biofeedback technology. Furthermore, optimizing operating room configurations and adopting advanced technologies like robotic systems and augmented reality (AR) may significantly reduce physical exertion, though they present their own unique ergonomic challenges.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Addressing surgical ergonomic challenges is vital for maintaining the physical and mental health of surgeons, ensuring the sustainability of healthcare provision and preventing attrition from surgical careers. Behavioral interventions are the cornerstone of a multifaceted approach to improving surgical ergonomics, encompassing physical adjustments, awareness training and policy development. Fostering a sustainable surgical workforce necessitates widespread awareness, formal ergonomic education and the integration of adaptive technologies and optimized operating environments.

items.title: Child-focused mHealth apps used in collaborative, real-world interventions: A scoping review.
items.authors: Pardal S, O'Hagan R, Abaya-Kotey E, Schnittker JA, Glista D.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The field of rehabilitation is experiencing an influx of mobile health (mHealth) applications designed to improve access to care and support adherence to therapeutic interventions. Rehabilitation encompasses a range of disciplines, including audiology, speech language pathology, clinical psychology, occupational and physical therapy, orthotics and prosthetics, and physical and rehabilitation medicine; each contributing to optimizing function and reducing disability for individuals with diverse health conditions. This scoping review aimed to synthesize the literature on pediatric-focused mHealth apps in real-world intervention studies led by rehabilitation healthcare professionals as part of a collaborative care practice.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A comprehensive search was conducted using MEDLINE(R) ALL (Ovid), Embase and Embase Classic (Ovid), Nursing and Allied Health, Web of Science, Scopus, and CINAHL (EBSCO) databases. A published protocol guided study selection and data extraction based on defined objectives and inclusion criteria.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Forty-five peer-reviewed articles met the inclusion criteria. The studies addressed pediatric health conditions related to speech and language, hearing, mental health, physical functioning, autism spectrum disorder, and developmental disorders. Identified mHealth apps incorporated both active (e.g., two-way communication, tailored interventions, data uploads, interactive prompts) and passive features (e.g., reminders, digital diaries, Bluetooth connectivity, one-way messaging).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This review demonstrates the emerging use of pediatric mHealth applications within collaborative rehabilitative models. Findings underscore the need for greater integration of mHealth tools into interprofessional pediatric rehabilitation and for the use of consistent evaluation frameworks to support equitable and evidence-based digital care.

items.title: Exploring ifosfamide-related central nervous system adverse events based on the FAERS database and clinical feature analysis of cases.
items.authors: Shi P, Mei Q, Zheng R, Wang S.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Ifosfamide, an alkylating agent used to treat various malignancies, has limited real-world safety data on neurotoxicity. Therefore, this study analyzed ifosfamide-related Central Nervous System Adverse Events (CNS AEs) to provide a reference for drug risk management.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The disproportionality study was performed leveraging the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database from 2004 to 2024. Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR), Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR), Multi-item Gamma Poisson Shrinker (MGPS), and Bayesian Information Component (IC) were applied to identify and evaluate potential CNS AEs associated with ifosfamide. The Weibull distribution was applied to characterize the risk of AEs over time. Case reports from PubMed and SpringerLink were reviewed to summarize the clinical characteristics of these AEs.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: This study identified 786 reports of ifosfamide-related CNS AEs. Disproportionality analysis revealed encephalopathy as the strongest signal (n=252, ROR = 101.19). Six label-unlisted adverse events were also identified, including brain oedema, hydrocephalus, spinal cord compression, cerebral ischemia, gaze palsy, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. The time-to-onset analysis revealed an early failure pattern with a median onset of 2 days after drug exposure. Brain oedema exhibited the highest mortality rate (83.33%). Subgroup analysis suggested greater susceptibility to encephalopathy in female patients and to confusion and coma in elderly patients. The systematic case review included 61 cases from 42 articles, involving patients aged 3-77 years. Therein, 46 (75.41%) cases experienced central neurotoxic reactions after receiving one to three cycles of ifosfamide-containing chemotherapy and the common clinical symptoms included impaired consciousness, hallucinations, seizures, delirium, disorientation, and various psychiatric or behavioral abnormalities.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: This study corroborates clinical observations by systematically characterizing the features of ifosfamide-related CNS toxicity and identifying potentially label-unlisted AEs, supporting further validation in prospective epidemiological studies.
