items.title: Methods for mapping population-level interventions in system dynamics modelling for context-sensitive policy planning in youth mental health.
items.authors: Loblay V, Ianelli O, Hindmarsh G, Song YJC, Huntley S, Piper S, Crosland P, Hosseini SH, Ho N, Nguyen KH, Vacher C, Hutcheon A, Rosenberg S, McNeill A, Oakes H, Occhipinti JA, B Hickie I.
items.journal: International journal of mental health systems

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Growing appreciation for the role of System Dynamics Modelling (SDM) in mental health decision-making is yet to translate into its widespread application. This article investigates why this is the case, aiming to identify and overcome barriers to its successful future use in supporting better decision-making.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We describe a three-stage participatory process developed iteratively across multiple regions in Australia: (1) identifying priority interventions through rapid evidence reviews and collaborating with stakeholders to understand regional needs and imminent funding decisions; (2) developing intervention-specific model parameters through the synthesis of research evidence and local contextual knowledge; and (3) using simulation scenarios as thinking tools to support critical reflection and deliberation on youth mental health investment strategies. We draw on an implementation narrative to demonstrate how this approach works in place-based regional planning practice.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The participatory processes built stakeholder capacity for systems thinking and enabled critical engagement with SDMs. Through exploring simulation scenarios, decision-makers developed appreciation for combining interventions versus implementing them separately; decision points shifted from questions of whether to fund interventions to strategic discussions about resource allocation and how to collaborate to achieve impact in the region. This methodology highlights the critical role of 'backstage work' beyond participatory workshops in which diverse forms of evidence and local contextual knowledge are translated into the formal SDM, building trust in the model while fostering capacity for model use.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: System Dynamics Models can be the thinking tools that support deliberative decision-making practices. Augmenting SDMs with local expertise through these participatory practices delivers an effective method to embed these models in regional mental health decision-making, for better resource allocation and strategic planning of local mental health services.

items.title: Association of genetic predisposition to immune-related biomarkers with premenstrual disorders and symptom severity.
items.authors: Luo Y, Sun J, Chen M, Pan Q, Pan T, Huang J, Song H, Li Y, Lu D.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Premenstrual disorders (PMD), including premenstrual syndrome (PMS) and the more severe premenstrual dysphoric disorder (PMDD), are burdensome conditions with unclear mechanisms. While inflammation is implicated, biomarker research is challenged by inconsistent findings and cyclical fluctuations. This study utilized polygenic risk scores (PRS) to investigate the association between lifelong genetic predisposition to altered immune-related cell counts and PMD risk and symptom severity.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This cross-sectional study included 1,730 Chinese college students from the Care of Premenstrual Emotion cohort. PRS were calculated for seven immune biomarkers: white blood cell (WBC), basophil, eosinophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, neutrophil, and C-reactive protein. Probable PMD cases and symptom severity (total, physical, affective) were assessed using a modified Calendar of Premenstrual Experiences. Generalized estimating equations estimated risk ratios (RR) and β-coefficients, adjusting for confounders.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Overall, 424 (24.5%) participants met probable PMD criteria, including 379 (21.9%) with PMS and 45 (2.6%) with PMDD. The PRS for WBC showed a suggestive, non-significant association with diagnosis (RR, 1.08; 95% CI, 1.00-1.18; P = 0.062). No other immune PRS showed significant associations. A higher PRS for WBC was associated with physical symptom severity (β = 0.05; 95% CI, 0.00-0.10; P = 0.047). This association was stronger in women with symptom onset at menarche (β = 0.47; 95% CI, 0.15-0.78; P = 0.008). The highest quintile of PRS for WBC exhibited greater severity across all domains versus the lowest, suggesting a possible graded pattern. Item-level analyses suggested signals for limb swelling, increased appetite, and food cravings.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The PRS for WBC may be associated with premenstrual symptom severity, specifically physical domains. These findings suggest that inflammatory liability may contribute to the physical symptom burden of PMD, but replication in prospectively phenotyped cohorts with detailed gynecologic and medical comorbidity data is needed.

items.title: Striatal dopamine transporter binding in adults with 22q11.2 copy number variants: a SPECT study.
items.authors: Spapens JCC, van Hooijdonk CF, Schalbroeck R, Sylvester AL, Boot E, van Amelsvoort TAMJ, Vingerhoets C, Booij J.

sections.text: Copy number variants at the 22q11.2 chromosomal locus, hemizygous 22q11.2 deletions or duplications, are associated with a broad spectrum of neuropsychiatric and other medical conditions. Individuals with a 22q11.2 deletion are at increased risk for developing early-onset Parkinson's disease. The catechol-O-methyltransferase gene at 22q11.2 is involved in dopamine metabolism. While previous studies have examined several aspects of dopamine function in individuals with 22q11.2 copy number variants, striatal dopamine transporter availability, a regulator of synaptic dopamine, has not yet been systematically investigated. Therefore, dopamine transporter availability was quantified in nine adults with a 22q11.2 deletion, nine with a 22q11.2 duplication and eight controls using a brain-dedicated single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) system. Specific striatal binding ratios were calculated with the occipital lobe as the reference region. Permutation analysis of covariance controlling for age and sex showed significantly higher striatal dopamine transporter availability in adults with 22q11.2 deletions compared with those with duplications ( P = 0.026, η ^2 _p = 0.30). No significant differences were observed between adults with 22q11.2 copy number variants and controls. These findings suggest distinct nigrostriatal dopaminergic profiles associated with 22q11.2 copy number variant status, which may play a role in shaping frequently occurring neurological and psychiatric phenotypes in these individuals.

items.title: Cross-sectoral gerontopsychiatric treatment and rehabilitation in nursing homes (SGB Reha)-study protocol for a stepped-wedge cluster randomized trial.
items.authors: Mierzwa N, Gradel B, Förstner BR, Deeken F, Desch A, Schroth JM, Du M, Dierbach O, Holmberg C, Hauptmann M, Rapp M, Häusler A.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Demographic changes in Germany have increased the need for care to 5.7 million people, with around 800,000 living in residential care facilities. Nursing home residents are vulnerable, suffering from multimorbidity and cognitive impairments, with prevalent use of psychotropic medication linked to negative outcomes like sedation and hospitalizations. So far, there is little research on multimodal rehabilitation programs in nursing homes. The SGB Reha study aims to implement a cross-sectoral rehabilitation model to improve activities of daily living (ADLs), cognition, and quality of life for nursing home residents, reducing hospitalizations and treatment costs, and increasing the chance of residents returning home post-care.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The study is conducted in 12 nursing homes located in North Rhine-Westphalia and Hamburg. It employs a cluster-randomized stepped-wedge design with randomization at the facility level. Data collection occurs at three consecutive measurement points, at 0, 3, and 6 months. The recruitment target includes 720 nursing home residents across four six-month study phases. Nursing home residents aged 65 years and older who had been admitted to the nursing home within the previous 12 months-either as a routine admission or following a hospital stay-and who have a care level of at least 2 are eligible for inclusion. The intervention integrates therapeutic and rehabilitative nursing practices. Structured multidisciplinary case conferences (including neurologists/psychiatrists, and consulting pharmacists) establish objectives, assess progress, adapt personalized care, develop therapeutic strategies, and systematically evaluate medications, especially emphasizing the reduction of psychotropic drugs and polypharmacy prevention. A multidisciplinary team delivers the intervention, supported by study nurses coordinating processes. In addition to resident outcomes, the study evaluates quality of life among relatives and job satisfaction among nursing home staff, allowing assessment of intervention effects across multiple stakeholder groups.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: The intervention aims to enhance ADLs, cognition, and quality of life for nursing home residents. By combining effectiveness, health-economic, qualitative, and process evaluations, the study adopts a health services perspective that extends beyond resident-level outcomes to include relatives, staff, organizational processes, and healthcare system implications. Results of the trial are intended to contribute to the further development of rehabilitation-oriented and gerontopsychiatric care structures in German nursing homes. From an economic perspective, we anticipate a reduction in treatment costs. This can contribute to a sustainable cross-sectoral care model that integrates therapeutic-rehabilitative approaches into standard care in residential long-term care.

sections.text: Recruitment and data collection are complete; analyses are ongoing (protocol reported after conclusion of data collection).

items.title: Three-year trajectories of insomnia symptoms among young breast cancer survivors.
items.authors: Hery CM, Williams K, Janse SA, Peng J, Kalam F, Van Zee K, Naftalis EZ, Paskett ED, Naughton MJ.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Sleep disruptions are common in cancer survivors and can negatively impact quality of life. Young breast cancer survivors face unique challenges and may have distinct sleep patterns. We examined trajectories of insomnia symptoms over 3 years among young survivors.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: 836 women, ≤45 years old with stage I-III breast cancer, were recruited to the Menstrual Cycle Maintenance and Quality of Life After Breast Cancer Study within 8 months of diagnosis. Insomnia symptoms were assessed at 6-month intervals from baseline through 3 years post-recruitment, using the Women's Health Initiative Insomnia Rating Scale (WHIIRS). Group-based trajectory modeling was used to identify distinct trajectories of insomnia symptoms. The final model was chosen by comparing the average posterior probability of assignment (PPA) and examining the distinctiveness and interpretability of the trajectories. Key demographic, quality of life and clinical variables were assessed in multinomial logistic regression models as potential factors associated with group membership.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The mean age of participants was 38 years (range: 20-45 years) at enrollment. Three distinct insomnia trajectories were identified: low probability of insomnia (n=277, 33.1%), moderate probability (n=354, 42.4%), and high probability (n=205, 24.5%). Average PPA was between 75%-82% for each group. Insomnia symptoms were highest at baseline but improved for the low probability and moderate probability groups. In adjusted models, older age (p=0.02), lower education (p=0.03), having received chemotherapy (p=0.03), night sweats (p=0.02), lower SF-12 physical component scores (poorer physical functioning, p<0.0001), and lower SF-12 mental health component scores (p<0.0001) were associated with participants in the moderate and high probability insomnia groups compared to those in the low probability group.

items.title: Relative importance of psychosocial and organizational predictors of burnout among European researchers: a dominance analysis.
items.authors: Noe MTN, Wild P, Mol ST, Guseva Canu I.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: Burnout is increasingly reported among researchers in European academia; however, the relative importance of its psychosocial and organizational determinants across career stages remains insufficiently understood. This study aimed to rank the relative importance of a defined set of predictors of burnout among junior and senior researchers.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Cross-sectional data were drawn from the European Researcher Mental Health Observatory (ReMO) Staircase survey ( N  = 4,026). Burnout was assessed using the 12-item Burnout Assessment Tool. Analyses were conducted separately for junior and senior researchers. Missing data were addressed using multiple imputation by chained equations. Dominance analysis estimated the relative importance of twelve predictors among junior researchers and ten among senior researchers based on their contribution to explained variance (R^2), with bootstrapped confidence intervals computed for all predictors.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The models explained substantial variance in burnout ( R^2  = 0.485 for junior researchers; R^2  = 0.515 for senior researchers). Resilience and role clarity emerged as the most important predictors in both groups, followed by work-family conflict and work-related stress. Illegitimate tasks showed somewhat greater dominance among senior researchers (in a comparison restricted to the ten predictors shared by both groups), while other predictors contributed similarly across career stages. Confidence intervals indicated that several mid-ranked predictors were not clearly separable from one another. The overall pattern of predictor dominance was broadly consistent across career stages and analytical approaches.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Burnout in academia reflects systemic features of modern higher education, including high workload, role ambiguity, administrative burden, and competitive evaluation systems. These results support a shift from individual-focused interventions toward structural reforms. A Total Worker Health approach is recommended, emphasizing improved role clarity, workload regulation, job stability, and more balanced reward systems to promote sustainable academic careers.

items.title: Impact of the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) Pandemic on Medical Interpreters: A Qualitative Focus Group Study.
items.authors: Melloy MP, Aziz F, Botsford C, Fong S, McPherson L, Freeman K.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic changed the health care experience, impacting medical interpreters and the non-English language preference (NELP) patients they serve. NELP patients experienced increased isolation, barriers to care, and worse health outcomes. Interpreters faced rapid changes in care provision, including high patient volumes, increased illness severity, and transition to virtual and remote care. We aim to explore the experience, challenges, and recommendations of medical interpreters providing care during the COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Five virtual focus groups, with a total of 24 professional medical interpreters, were conducted using a semi-structured guide. Transcripts were then coded for thematic analysis with an iterative debriefing process to refine codes and themes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The challenges faced by participants during the COVID-19 pandemic included a rapid transition to remote interpretation, personal and patient safety concerns, elevated mental and emotional burden, and limited institutional support. Despite these challenges, participants felt immense pride in their role and the care provided. They describe limited opportunities for connection and support and a lack of professional recognition and detailed opportunities to further support interpreters in the future.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Interpreters identified challenges in adapting to virtual and remote work, ensuring safety and quality of care, and maintaining mental health.

sections.heading: Health equity implications
sections.text: Interpreters suggest developing further health care worker training, highlighting best practices for NELP and interpreted visits, supporting interpreter professional development, and increasing interpreter visibility and recognition as next steps to improve care quality. Further insight into the perspective of NELP patients is needed to support high-quality, equitable patient care.

items.title: Development, Expert Validation, and Feasibility Testing of a Psychological Resilience Reinforcement Programme for Omani University Students: A Pilot Quasi-Experimental Study.
items.authors: Yesodharan DK, Arulappan J, S S, Sridhar O T S.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: University students face significant mental health challenges that may be mitigated by strengthening their resilience. However, resilience-building programs for this population remain underexplored.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This feasibility pilot trial aimed to develop, validate, and explore the feasibility of a psychological resilience reinforcement programme for university students in Oman, with an exploratory evaluation of psychological outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A quasi-experimental, non-randomised design with two parallel groups; control and intervention was employed. Eligible students were conveniently recruited between November 2023 and February 2024 and allocated non-randomly. The intervention group (n = 25) completed two 45-minute sessions, while the control group (n = 25) received no intervention. The programme, grounded in positive psychology principles, included active coping, emotional awareness, self-regulation, impulse control, optimism, empathy, self-efficacy, challenging thinking traps, and the importance of social connections. Psychological well-being, coping, and psychological resilience were assessed at baseline, immediately after the intervention, and at three-month follow-up.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The programme achieved a content validity index of 0.94, demonstrating excellent feasibility and acceptability, with 100% recruitment, retention, data completion, and follow-up rates and no reported adverse events. Exploratory, descriptive analysis revealed temporal changes in well-being (F (1.77,84.94) = 5.13, p = 0.008, ηp2 = 0.01) and coping (F (1.20,57.52) = 10.24, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.18), but no statistically significant effects for resilience. However, these findings are exploratory, not causal.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The programme exhibited strong content validity and feasibility; however, no statistically significant effect on psychological outcomes was observed. Changes observed over time, including decline at three months are likely attributable to contextual influences rather than effect of the intervention. Findings suggest the need for a fully powered trial to evaluate effectiveness. This non-funded trial was registered with the Iranian Trial Registry.
